title: Complexity Classes: P and NP
tagline: P vs NP — the most important open problem in computer science. Can every problem whose answer is easy to verify also be solved efficiently?

sections.content:
Imagine you receive a completed Sudoku puzzle. Checking whether the solution is valid takes a few seconds — you scan rows, columns, and boxes. But if you receive a blank puzzle, finding the solution could take hours. This gap between **checking** and **finding** is the deepest mystery in theoretical computer science, and it sits at the heart of a question that has stumped the world's best mathematicians for over fifty years: **does P equal NP?**

**Complexity theory** is the branch of computer science that classifies computational problems not just by whether they can be solved, but by *how much resource it costs to solve them*. The most important resources are time and space. Two central complexity classes dominate this landscape: **P**, the class of problems solvable by an efficient algorithm (one that runs in polynomial time), and **NP**, the class of problems whose solutions can be *verified* efficiently even if finding them seems hard.

Every problem in P is trivially in NP — if you can find a solution quickly, you can certainly check one quickly. The question is whether the reverse holds: does the ability to verify solutions quickly imply the ability to find them quickly? Most computer scientists believe the answer is **no** — that P ≠ NP — but no proof exists. This is one of the seven **Millennium Prize Problems**, each carrying a one-million-dollar reward from the Clay Mathematics Institute.

The practical stakes are enormous. Thousands of real problems — from scheduling airline crews to optimising supply chains to breaking encryption — fall into the class of **NP-complete** problems: the hardest problems in NP, where a breakthrough on any one would immediately solve all of them. Understanding complexity classes helps you recognise when a problem is fundamentally hard, choose the right coping strategy, and appreciate why modern cryptography works at all.

sections.title: The Crossword Puzzle Principle
sections.content:
Think about three everyday activities that capture the essence of these complexity classes perfectly.

**Arithmetic** represents **P**: computing 17 × 23 is fast and systematic. You have a reliable, step-by-step procedure — long multiplication — that always produces the answer in a predictable amount of work. Both *finding* and *checking* the answer are quick.

**Sudoku** represents **NP**: given a completed grid, checking validity is trivial — just scan each row, column, and 3×3 box for duplicate digits. But *finding* the solution for a blank puzzle is a different matter. You might try a digit, discover a contradiction 20 steps later, and need to backtrack and try again. The search space is vast. No one has found a reliable procedure that is as fast as the checker.

**Generalised chess** represents a problem believed to lie **beyond NP**: 'does White have a forced win from this position on an n×n board?' is EXPTIME-complete. Someone claiming 'yes' cannot hand you a short certificate — a winning *strategy* must answer every possible reply, and checking it is as hard as solving the game. For such problems even verification offers no shortcut.

The P vs NP question asks: is Sudoku secretly more like arithmetic? Is there a slick trick we have missed for more than 50 years that would let us solve Sudoku as efficiently as we check it? The overwhelming consensus is no — but consensus is not proof.

sections.title: Defining P: Polynomial Time and Why It Matters
sections.content:
**P** (polynomial time) is the class of **decision problems** solvable by a deterministic algorithm in time O(nᵏ) for some constant k, where n is the input size. A decision problem is one with a yes/no answer — 'is there a path of length ≤ k in this graph?' rather than 'what is the shortest path?'

Polynomial time is the formal definition of 'efficient' (the Cobham–Edmonds thesis). Why polynomials and not, say, O(n log n) only? Because polynomial functions compose nicely: running two polynomial-time algorithms sequentially or in parallel gives another polynomial-time algorithm. Also, the difference between O(n²) and O(n³) is manageable in practice; the difference between O(n³) and O(2ⁿ) is catastrophic even for moderate n.

Consider n = 1000 (a small input): n² = 1,000,000 (fast on any modern computer); 2ⁿ = 2¹⁰⁰⁰, a number with 302 digits — more operations than atoms in the observable universe, no matter how fast the hardware.

Problems in P include: **Sorting** (O(n log n) — merge sort, quicksort); **Shortest path in a weighted graph** (Dijkstra O(E log V), Bellman-Ford O(VE)); **Minimum spanning tree** (Kruskal O(E log E), Prim O(E log V)); **Primality testing** (the AKS algorithm, published in 2002, runs in Õ(b⁶) for a b-bit number in its improved Lenstra–Pomerance form — a major breakthrough proving primality is in P, though Miller–Rabin is what everyone actually uses); **Maximum bipartite matching** (Hopcroft-Karp O(E√V)); **Linear programming** (ellipsoid method, interior-point methods — polynomial but not the simplex method, which is exponential in the worst case).

The rough rule of thumb: if a problem has a well-known named algorithm in every algorithms textbook, it is probably in P.

sections.title: Defining NP: Certificates and Verification
sections.content:
**NP** (Non-deterministic Polynomial time) is the class of decision problems where, for every 'yes' instance, there exists a **certificate** (a proposed solution) that can be *verified* in polynomial time by a deterministic algorithm.

The word 'Non-deterministic' comes from an equivalent alternative definition: NP = problems solvable in polynomial time by a **non-deterministic Turing machine** — a theoretical machine that can simultaneously explore all possible paths of computation and accepts if *any* path leads to acceptance. Think of it as magically 'guessing' the right certificate and then checking it. The verification step takes polynomial time; the guessing step is the non-deterministic 'free gift'.

**Critical common misconception**: NP does NOT stand for 'Not Polynomial'. Problems in NP might also be in P — indeed, P ⊆ NP. The 'N' means Non-deterministic. Calling a problem 'NP' does not mean it is hard; it means we know its solutions can be checked quickly.

**The certificate model in practice**: For the Boolean Satisfiability Problem (SAT), the certificate is a truth assignment to variables. For the Clique problem, the certificate is the set of vertices claimed to form the clique. For Subset Sum, the certificate is the subset itself. In each case, you can verify the certificate in time linear or polynomial in the input size — you just check the claimed solution without needing to search for it.

An important subtlety: NP is defined only for 'yes' instances. For a 'no' instance, there is no requirement that a short certificate of non-existence exists. The class **co-NP** contains problems where 'no' instances have polynomial-time verifiable certificates. Whether NP = co-NP is another famous open question, and most experts believe they are different.

sections.title: Polynomial-Time Reductions: Proving Relative Hardness
sections.content:
The most powerful tool in complexity theory is the **polynomial-time reduction**. A reduction from problem A to problem B (written A ≤ₚ B, read 'A reduces to B') is a polynomial-time computable function f such that:

x ∈ A  ↔  f(x) ∈ B

In plain English: any instance of A can be transformed into an equivalent instance of B in polynomial time, preserving yes/no answers. If you can solve B efficiently, you can solve A efficiently: first transform the A-instance to a B-instance, solve B, and report the same answer.

The power of reductions flows in the **contrapositive direction**: if A is known to be hard and A ≤ₚ B, then B must also be hard. B is at least as hard as A. This is the standard technique for proving NP-hardness: show that a known NP-hard problem reduces to your new problem.

**NP-hardness** means every problem in NP reduces to it in polynomial time. A problem H is NP-hard if for every problem L in NP, L ≤ₚ H. Solving H would solve all of NP.

**NP-completeness** = NP-hard AND in NP. These are the problems that sit at the very frontier of tractability — they are the hardest problems you can still efficiently verify. If any single NP-complete problem could be solved in polynomial time, every NP problem could, because you could reduce any NP problem to that one NP-complete problem and then solve it.

The question P vs NP asks precisely: is any NP-complete problem in P?

sections.title: Cook's Theorem: The First NP-Complete Problem
sections.content:
In 1971, Stephen Cook (and independently, Leonid Levin in the Soviet Union, published 1973) proved the first NP-completeness result: **Boolean Satisfiability (SAT) is NP-complete**. This was a landmark — it established that NP-complete problems exist and gave the first benchmark for reductions.

**SAT** asks: given a propositional formula (a Boolean formula using AND, OR, NOT), does there exist a truth assignment to its variables that makes the formula true (satisfies it)?

Example: (x₁ ∨ x₂) ∧ (¬x₁ ∨ x₃) ∧ (¬x₂ ∨ ¬x₃). Setting x₁=true, x₂=false, x₃=true satisfies all three clauses. This particular instance is satisfiable.

Cook proved SAT is in NP (obvious — a truth assignment is a polynomial-time verifiable certificate) and, more remarkably, that *every problem in NP reduces to SAT in polynomial time*. The proof encodes any non-deterministic Turing machine computation as a Boolean formula, so that a satisfying assignment corresponds to an accepting computation path. This is the hardest direction and required deep insight about the structure of computation itself.

Richard Karp (1972) then showed 21 problems NP-complete through chains of reductions starting from SAT, and the floodgates opened. Today, thousands of NP-complete problems are known across combinatorics, graph theory, scheduling, cryptography, and biology.

A critical special case: **3-SAT** restricts SAT to formulas in **conjunctive normal form (CNF)** where every clause has exactly 3 literals. 3-SAT is also NP-complete (proved by reducing general SAT to it) and is the most common starting point for new reductions because its rigid structure makes reductions easier to design. Note that **2-SAT** (clauses with at most 2 literals) is in P — proved by converting to an implication graph and finding strongly connected components in O(V+E).

sections.caption: The NP-completeness reduction chain. SAT is the root (Cook's theorem). Each arrow represents a polynomial-time reduction — a new problem is proved NP-complete by transforming it from an already-known NP-complete problem. This chain now extends to thousands of problems.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The verifier scans each clause once — O(clauses × literals), clearly polynomial. The solver must enumerate all 2ⁿ possible truth assignments because no smarter strategy is known. For 3 variables, this is fine. For 100 variables it is astronomically infeasible — 2¹⁰⁰ ≈ 1.3 × 10³⁰ checks would take about 4 × 10¹³ years at a billion checks per second. (Real SAT solvers do far better than brute force on most practical instances — see the coping strategies below — but no known algorithm avoids exponential worst-case time.) This exponential vs polynomial gap is the practical meaning of NP-completeness.

sections.title: A Canonical Gallery of NP-Complete Problems
sections.content:
Once Cook proved SAT was NP-complete, Karp (1972) proved 21 more problems NP-complete in a single paper. Here is a tour of the most important ones and why they matter:

**Vertex Cover**: Given graph G and integer k, does G have a set of at most k vertices such that every edge is incident to at least one? Applications: network monitoring (which routers must observe all links?), facility location. Proved NP-complete by reduction from 3-SAT via Independent Set.

**Clique**: Does G contain a complete subgraph of size ≥ k? Applications: social network analysis (find groups where everyone knows everyone), bioinformatics (common subgraph detection). Vertex Cover, Clique, and Independent Set are all equivalent under complement: a set S is a vertex cover iff V\S is an independent set; S is an independent set iff S is a clique in the complement graph.

**Hamiltonian Cycle / Path**: Does a graph have a cycle (or path) that visits every vertex exactly once? This is the combinatorial core of the **Travelling Salesman Problem (TSP)**. Proved NP-complete by reduction from 3-SAT. Note: finding an *Eulerian* cycle (visiting every *edge* exactly once) is in P — solvable by Hierholzer's O(E) algorithm. One letter difference (vertex vs edge) separates P from NP-complete.

**Subset Sum**: Given integers S = {s₁, …, sₙ} and target t, does some subset sum to exactly t? Directly relevant to: knapsack problems, coin change (general case), bin packing. The simple special case where all numbers are 1 is trivially in P.

**Graph k-Colouring (k ≥ 3)**: Can graph vertices be assigned one of k colours so no adjacent vertices share a colour? 2-Colouring (bipartite testing) is in P via BFS. 3-Colouring is NP-complete. Applications: register allocation in compilers (k = number of registers), map colouring, scheduling conflicts.

**TSP (decision)**: Given cities with distances, is there a tour visiting all cities with total length ≤ k? The optimisation version ('find the shortest tour') is NP-hard but not in NP — NP contains only yes/no decision problems, and even the related question 'is this particular tour optimal?' has no known short certificate. TSP with triangle inequality (metric TSP) admits a 1.5-approximation (Christofides algorithm, improved to 1.5 − 10⁻³⁶ in 2020); general TSP cannot be approximated within any constant factor unless P = NP.

**Boolean Circuit Satisfiability (CircuitSAT)**: Is there an input that makes a given Boolean circuit output 1? Many textbooks prove CircuitSAT NP-complete first (it mirrors the hardware of a verifier directly) and then reduce it to SAT. Any formula is a special case of a circuit.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The verifier is polynomial — check membership and sum. The brute-force solver is O(2ⁿ). The dynamic programming solution runs in O(n × target), which looks polynomial but is actually **pseudo-polynomial** — 'target' can itself be exponentially large in the number of bits used to encode it. This distinction between weak and strong NP-completeness matters for algorithm design: pseudo-polynomial DP works when target values are small (e.g., change-making for small denominations), but fails for large encoded numbers.

sections.title: Coping with NP-Completeness: Four Strategies
sections.content:
Proving a problem NP-complete is not the end of the story — it is the beginning of a more nuanced engineering conversation. In practice, NP-complete problems are solved every day. Here are the four main strategies:

**Strategy 1: Approximation algorithms** — Find a solution guaranteed to be within a factor α of optimal in polynomial time. Classic examples: the **2-approximation for Vertex Cover** (greedily pick uncovered edges, add both endpoints — O(E), always within 2× optimal); the **1.5-approximation for metric TSP** (Christofides algorithm, 1976 — minimum spanning tree plus minimum-weight perfect matching on odd-degree vertices); a **PTAS (polynomial-time approximation scheme)** for Euclidean TSP (Arora 1998 — for any ε > 0, runs in n^O(1/ε) time with solution within (1+ε)× optimal). Some problems are **APX-hard** — they have no PTAS unless P = NP.

**Strategy 2: Exact exponential algorithms with pruning** — For small n or structured inputs, branch-and-bound, backtracking with constraint propagation, or modern **CDCL (Conflict-Driven Clause Learning)** SAT solvers work phenomenally well in practice. Industrial SAT solvers — MiniSat and Glucose historically, Kissat and CaDiCaL at the top of recent SAT competitions — routinely handle instances with millions of variables by learning and caching conflict clauses. The theoretical worst case is exponential, but the average case on real inputs can be much better.

**Strategy 3: Fixed-parameter tractability (FPT)** — Parameterised algorithms run in O(f(k) · nᶜ) where k is a 'natural' small parameter and c is a constant. Example: Vertex Cover parameterised by cover size k has an O(2ᵏ · n) FPT algorithm — exponential in k but polynomial in n. If k is small (say, ≤ 30), this is entirely practical. The field of **parameterised complexity** studies which parameters make which problems tractable.

**Strategy 4: Exploit special structure** — The general case may be NP-complete, but your specific instance may have structure that makes it tractable. Examples: TSP on the Euclidean plane (uses geometric properties); Graph colouring on planar graphs (4-colorable by the Four-Color Theorem, and 3-colorability is still NP-complete but structure helps); Scheduling problems where all jobs have equal length. Before declaring a problem NP-complete for your use case, check whether your inputs have special structure.

sections.title: The Implications of P = NP vs P ≠ NP
sections.content:
The P vs NP question is not merely academic — its resolution would have sweeping consequences for mathematics, science, and society.

**If P = NP (the surprising case, believed unlikely)**:

Every NP-complete problem would be solvable in polynomial time. This sounds wonderful, but the immediate consequences would be destabilising:

- **Cryptography collapses**: Modern public-key cryptography (RSA, elliptic curve, Diffie-Hellman) relies on the apparent hardness of problems like integer factorisation and the discrete logarithm problem. These are believed to be NP-intermediate (neither in P nor NP-complete). But their decision versions are in NP, so a proof that P = NP would put factoring and discrete log in P outright. Whether that breaks encryption *in practice* depends on the algorithm: a 'galactic' O(n¹⁰⁰) algorithm would be a theoretical earthquake but no practical threat. Every secure communication, every HTTPS website, every digital signature would be theoretically breakable.

- **Combinatorial optimisation becomes tractable**: TSP, protein folding, drug design, logistics scheduling, genome assembly — all solved in polynomial time. Massive scientific breakthroughs would follow.

- **Mathematics would be automated**: Theorem proving is closely related to NP. A P = NP proof might enable computers to efficiently find proofs of mathematical conjectures.

**If P ≠ NP (the expected case)**:

- The status quo of cryptography is justified — hard problems remain hard.
- NP-complete problems remain intractable at large scale, and we must rely on the four coping strategies above.
- The intellectual challenge of proving P ≠ NP remains open. Known barriers (relativisation, natural proofs, algebrisation) rule out whole families of proof techniques — the proof will require genuinely new mathematics.

**The landscape of related questions**: Beyond P vs NP, complexity theory asks many related questions. Is NP = co-NP (do 'no' instances also have polynomial certificates)? What is the power of randomisation — is BPP = P (can derandomisation always remove randomness)? What about quantum computation — does NP ⊆ BQP? Most experts think not: Shor's algorithm breaks factoring, but no quantum algorithm is known for NP-complete problems. These questions collectively map the terrain of what is and is not computationally feasible.

sections.title: NP-Intermediate: The Space Between P and NP-Complete
sections.content:
If P ≠ NP, then by **Ladner's theorem** (1975), there must exist problems in NP that are neither in P nor NP-complete. This middle ground is called **NP-intermediate**. No problem has been *proven* NP-intermediate, but several are widely believed to be:

**Integer Factorisation**: Given n, find a non-trivial factor. Its decision version — 'does n have a factor ≤ k?' — is in NP (the factor is the certificate) and also in co-NP (the full prime factorisation is a certificate for 'no': multiply it out, and check each part is prime in polynomial time with AKS). An NP-complete problem in co-NP would imply NP = co-NP, which is one more reason experts doubt factoring is NP-complete. It is not known to be NP-complete, and most experts believe it is not. The entire RSA cryptosystem bets on its hardness.

**Discrete Logarithm**: Given g, h, p (prime), find x such that gˣ ≡ h (mod p). Similar status to factorisation — the basis for Diffie-Hellman and elliptic curve cryptography.

**Graph Isomorphism**: Given two graphs, are they isomorphic (identical up to relabelling of vertices)? In NP trivially (an isomorphism is a polynomial-time verifiable certificate). Not known to be in P or NP-complete. A quasi-polynomial algorithm by Babai (2015) — O(exp(polylog n)) — is a recent landmark but not polynomial.

The existence of NP-intermediate problems would mean that P ≠ NP creates a rich three-tier landscape: P (easy), NP-intermediate (hard but not hardest), and NP-complete (the hardest verifiable problems).

sections.title: Beyond NP: PSPACE, EXPTIME, and What Is Actually Proven
sections.content:
P and NP are two rooms in a larger building. The chain everyone should know is:

**P ⊆ NP ⊆ PSPACE ⊆ EXPTIME**

- **PSPACE**: problems solvable with a polynomial amount of *memory* (time may be exponential). Deciding the winner of generalised geography, or the truth of a quantified Boolean formula (∀x ∃y …), is PSPACE-complete.
- **EXPTIME**: problems solvable in time 2^poly(n). Generalised chess and Go (with suitable rules) are EXPTIME-complete.

Here is the striking part: we know **P ≠ EXPTIME** (the time hierarchy theorem proves more time lets you solve strictly more problems), so at least one of the inclusions above is strict — yet nobody can prove *which* one. P ≠ NP, NP ≠ PSPACE, and PSPACE ≠ EXPTIME are all open.

Randomness gets its own class: **BPP** (polynomial time with bounded error probability). Since primality moved from 'only randomised' to P via AKS, and strong circuit lower bounds would imply full derandomisation, most theorists now conjecture **BPP = P** — randomness is a practical convenience, not extra power.

**co-NP** mirrors NP for 'no' answers: UNSAT, TAUTOLOGY ('is this formula true under every assignment?') are co-NP-complete. If any NP-complete problem were in co-NP, then NP = co-NP.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The decision order mirrors how experienced engineers approach an NP-hard problem: tiny inputs → brute force; a small natural parameter → an exact FPT algorithm; need a guarantee → an approximation algorithm with a proven ratio; constraint-heavy → a SAT/SMT or MILP solver that is exponential in the worst case but fast on real instances. The 2-SAT vs 3-SAT contrast is one of the most striking illustrations in complexity theory — one extra literal per clause separates a linear-time problem from an NP-complete one.

sections.title: Brief History and Context: Why This Problem Is So Hard to Solve
sections.content:
The P vs NP question was first posed by Kurt Gödel in a 1956 letter to John von Neumann, where he asked whether mathematical theorem proving could be mechanised efficiently. The formal complexity-theoretic framing emerged from Cook's 1971 theorem and Karp's 1972 reductions.

Over fifty years of effort has produced no proof of P ≠ NP. This is not for lack of trying — some of the world's best mathematicians have attempted it, and the Clay Mathematics Institute added it to the Millennium Prize list in 2000 with a $1,000,000 reward.

The difficulty stems from fundamental barriers, formally identified by complexity theorists:

**Relativisation (Baker, Gill, Solovay, 1975)**: There exist oracle machines A and B such that Pᴬ = NPᴬ and Pᴮ ≠ NPᴮ. This means that any proof of P ≠ NP must be **non-relativising** — it cannot work by purely diagonalisation arguments (which would also work relative to oracles). Most classical proofs in computability theory relativise, so this rules out a huge class of proof techniques.

**Natural Proofs (Razborov and Rudich, 1994)**: Most combinatorial lower-bound techniques that could prove circuit lower bounds (a proxy for P ≠ NP) have a property called 'naturalness'. If strong one-way functions exist — which is widely believed, and which would itself imply P ≠ NP — then natural proofs cannot prove superpolynomial circuit lower bounds. A catch-22: if P ≠ NP, natural proof techniques cannot prove it.

**Algebrisation (Aaronson and Wigderson, 2009)**: An extension of relativisation — even algebraic extensions of oracle arguments are insufficient.

These barriers mean that a proof of P ≠ NP will require a fundamentally new mathematical technique, one that is simultaneously non-relativising, non-natural, and non-algebrising. This is part of why the problem is considered so deep.

**NP is not the same as 'unsolvable'**: A common misconception is that NP means 'impossible'. NP problems are perfectly solvable — just not efficiently for all large inputs. Every NP-complete problem with 10 variables can be solved by hand. The issue is scaling: with 1000 variables, the 2¹⁰⁰⁰ search space overwhelms any computer. Also remember: **co-NP** contains problems where 'no' instances have short certificates. The complement of SAT (UNSAT — is a formula unsatisfiable?) is in co-NP. Whether NP = co-NP is a separate open question, and most experts believe they differ.

**Interview and exam patterns to know cold**: (1) 'NP means Non-deterministic Polynomial, not Not Polynomial — P ⊆ NP.' (2) 'Reduction direction: to prove your problem X is NP-hard, reduce a known NP-complete problem *to* X (known ≤ₚ X). Reducing X to SAT only shows X is in NP.' (3) '2-SAT is P; 3-SAT is NP-complete — one extra literal per clause changes everything.' (4) 'Hamiltonian cycle is NP-complete; Eulerian cycle is O(E) — vertex vs edge makes the difference.' (5) 'TSP optimisation is NP-hard but not in NP; TSP decision (is there a tour ≤ k?) is NP-complete.' (6) 'Subset Sum has a pseudo-polynomial O(n·W) DP — weakly NP-complete; problems like 3-Partition, bin packing, and TSP stay NP-complete even with small numbers — strongly NP-complete.' (7) 'Proving NP-completeness tells your team: do not search for a polynomial exact algorithm — pivot to approximation, heuristics, or parameterisation.'

items: **P** = decision problems solvable by a deterministic algorithm in polynomial time O(nᵏ). **NP** = problems where a proposed solution (certificate) can be *verified* in polynomial time. P ⊆ NP; whether P = NP is the central open problem in computer science.
**NP does NOT mean 'Not Polynomial'** — the N stands for Non-deterministic. Problems in NP might well be in P too. The confusion is one of the most common misconceptions in computer science.

**NP-complete** = NP-hard ∩ NP. A problem is NP-hard if every NP problem reduces to it in polynomial time. NP-complete problems are simultaneously the hardest in NP and still efficiently verifiable. Cook's theorem (1971) proved SAT was the first NP-complete problem.

**Polynomial-time reductions** (A ≤ₚ B) are the core proof tool: if A reduces to B and A is hard, then B is hard. To prove a new problem X is NP-complete: show X ∈ NP, then reduce a known NP-complete problem (typically 3-SAT) **to X** — never the other way round.

Classic NP-complete problems include: **SAT, 3-SAT, Vertex Cover, Clique, Independent Set, Hamiltonian Cycle, TSP (decision), Subset Sum, Graph 3-Colouring**. 2-SAT and 2-Colouring are in P — special structure creates tractability.

**The bigger map**: P ⊆ NP ⊆ PSPACE ⊆ EXPTIME, and P ≠ EXPTIME is proven, so some inclusion is strict — but which one is unknown. Factoring and graph isomorphism are the best-known NP-intermediate candidates.

**Four coping strategies** for NP-complete problems in practice: (1) approximation algorithms with provable ratios; (2) exact exponential solvers with pruning (CDCL SAT solvers) for small/structured inputs; (3) fixed-parameter tractable (FPT) algorithms; (4) exploit special problem structure.

P = NP would collapse cryptography and enable efficient optimisation across science; P ≠ NP (the expected outcome) justifies cryptographic hardness and means NP-complete problems require the four coping strategies. Known proof barriers (relativisation, natural proofs, algebrisation) imply the proof will require fundamentally new mathematics.

quiz.question: What does NP stand for, and what is the correct definition of NP?
options: Not Polynomial — problems that cannot be solved in polynomial time.
Non-deterministic Polynomial — problems where a proposed solution (certificate) can be verified in polynomial time by a deterministic algorithm.
Nearly Polynomial — problems that run in O(n log n) or O(n²) but not O(n).
Negative Polynomial — problems whose complement is in P.
quiz.explanation: NP stands for Non-deterministic Polynomial. The defining property is that a proposed solution (certificate) can be verified in polynomial time. Equivalently, NP = problems solvable in polynomial time by a non-deterministic Turing machine. NP does NOT mean 'not polynomial' — this is one of the most common misconceptions. Problems in P are also in NP, since if you can solve a problem fast, you can verify a solution fast.

quiz.question: What does it mean for a problem to be NP-complete?
options: It is the easiest problem in NP — solvable faster than other NP problems.
It cannot be verified in polynomial time and has no known algorithm.
It is in P and can be reduced to any NP problem in polynomial time.
It is in NP and every problem in NP can be reduced to it in polynomial time, making it simultaneously the hardest verifiable problem.
quiz.explanation: NP-complete = NP-hard ∩ NP. A problem is NP-hard if every NP problem reduces to it in polynomial time (so solving it efficiently would solve all of NP). It is NP-complete if it is also IN NP — its solutions can be verified in polynomial time. NP-complete problems are the hardest problems in NP. If any one of them were in P, then P = NP.

quiz.question: Cook's theorem (1971) proved which problem is NP-complete, and why was this significant?
options: Boolean Satisfiability (SAT) — because it was the first NP-completeness proof, showing every NP problem encodes as a Boolean formula.
The Halting Problem — because it established limits of computability.
Travelling Salesman Problem (TSP) — because it is the most practically important NP-complete problem.
Graph 3-Colouring — because map colouring had been studied for centuries.
quiz.explanation: Cook proved SAT is NP-complete. The difficult direction was showing every NP problem reduces to SAT — achieved by encoding any non-deterministic Turing machine computation as a Boolean formula. This created the benchmark from which Karp (1972) reduced 21 more problems, establishing the reduction-chain methodology that now covers thousands of NP-complete problems.

quiz.question: Why is 2-SAT in P while 3-SAT is NP-complete?
options: 2-SAT has fewer variables, so the search space is smaller.
3-SAT uses larger integer coefficients which make it harder.
2-SAT converts to an implication graph solvable by strongly connected components in O(V+E); 3-SAT lacks this polynomial structure.
2-SAT is not actually in NP, so it cannot be NP-complete.
quiz.explanation: Each 2-SAT clause (a ∨ b) is equivalent to two implications (¬a → b) and (¬b → a). The resulting directed implication graph can be solved by finding strongly connected components using Tarjan's or Kosaraju's algorithm in O(V+E) — polynomial. The formula is unsatisfiable exactly when some variable x has x and ¬x in the same SCC (each would force the other); otherwise a satisfying assignment can be read off the SCC order. 3-SAT clauses do not decompose into pairwise implications, and 3-SAT is NP-complete.

quiz.question: What is a polynomial-time reduction (A ≤ₚ B) and what does it prove?
options: A polynomial-time algorithm that solves A by using B as a black-box subroutine.
A compression of B's running time to make it polynomial when solving A.
A proof that A and B have the same number of solutions.
A polynomial-time function f that maps instances of A to instances of B, preserving yes/no answers — proving B is at least as hard as A.
quiz.explanation: A ≤ₚ B means there is a polynomial-time computable function f where x ∈ A iff f(x) ∈ B. Crucially, if B is solvable in polynomial time, then so is A (transform A-instance to B-instance, solve B, report same answer). Contrapositively, if A is hard, B must be at least as hard. This asymmetry makes reductions the standard tool for proving NP-hardness: start from a known NP-hard problem (like 3-SAT) and reduce it to your new problem.

quiz.question: Which of the following is NP-complete while its closely related variant is in P?
options: Shortest path vs longest path — both NP-complete
Hamiltonian cycle (visit every vertex once) vs Eulerian cycle (visit every edge once) — Hamiltonian is NP-complete, Eulerian is O(E)
Sorting vs searching — sorting is NP-complete, searching is P
Primality testing vs factorisation — both are in P
quiz.explanation: Hamiltonian cycle (does a graph have a cycle visiting every vertex exactly once?) is NP-complete. Eulerian cycle (does a graph have a cycle traversing every edge exactly once?) is solvable in O(E) by Hierholzer's algorithm — just check that every vertex has even degree and the graph is connected. The vertex vs edge distinction is one of the most elegant P vs NP-complete contrasts. Primality is in P (AKS), but factorisation is believed NP-intermediate.

quiz.question: If someone proved P = NP tomorrow, what would be the most immediate consequence?
options: No practical consequences — only theoretical proofs would change.
The Halting Problem would become decidable.
Modern public-key cryptography (RSA, ECC) would be theoretically breakable, and NP-complete problems like SAT and TSP would be solvable in polynomial time.
All NP problems would move into co-NP, making them harder to verify.
quiz.explanation: P = NP would mean every NP-complete problem (SAT, TSP, graph colouring) has a polynomial-time algorithm. Cryptographic systems like RSA rely on problems (factorisation, discrete log) conjectured to be hard. Their decision versions are in NP, so P = NP would put them in P outright — making current public-key infrastructure theoretically breakable (how practical that would be depends on the actual algorithm). Every NP-complete optimisation problem (drug discovery, scheduling, logistics) would also become tractable.

quiz.question: What is the Christofides algorithm and why is it notable?
options: A 1.5-approximation algorithm for metric TSP running in polynomial time, using minimum spanning tree plus minimum-weight perfect matching on odd-degree vertices.
An exact polynomial-time TSP solver — proves TSP ∈ P for metric instances.
An NP-completeness proof for TSP showing it cannot be approximated within any constant factor.
A linear-time heuristic for general TSP with no proven approximation ratio.
quiz.explanation: Christofides (1976) gives a polynomial-time algorithm (O(n³)) that produces a TSP tour for metric instances (where triangle inequality holds) guaranteed within 1.5× the optimal. It works by: (1) compute minimum spanning tree, (2) find minimum-weight perfect matching on odd-degree MST vertices, (3) combine and shortcut to form a Hamiltonian cycle. Since exact TSP is NP-hard, a guaranteed approximation is the practical goal. Christofides' 1.5 ratio stood as the best known for over four decades, until Karlin, Klein and Oveis Gharan's (1.5 − 10⁻³⁶) improvement in 2020.

quiz.question: What is the difference between NP-hard and NP-complete, and give an example of each?
options: NP-hard problems are in NP; NP-complete problems are not in NP.
NP-complete = NP-hard ∩ NP. NP-hard problems need not be in NP. Example: SAT is NP-complete; the Halting Problem is NP-hard but not in NP (undecidable).
NP-hard and NP-complete are synonymous — both mean the hardest problems in NP.
NP-hard problems are harder than NP-complete; NP-complete problems have polynomial approximations while NP-hard do not.
quiz.explanation: NP-complete = NP-hard ∩ NP. An NP-hard problem H requires that every NP problem reduces to H in polynomial time — H is at least as hard as everything in NP. NP-complete additionally requires H to be IN NP (its solutions are efficiently verifiable). The Halting Problem is NP-hard (you could use a Halting oracle to solve any NP problem) but is undecidable and definitely not in NP. TSP optimisation (find minimum cost tour) is NP-hard but not in NP — the decision version (tour ≤ k?) is NP-complete.

quiz.question: What is Ladner's theorem and why does it matter for the P vs NP question?
options: It proves P ≠ NP using a diagonalisation argument.
It establishes that every NP-complete problem can be approximated within a constant factor.
It shows NP = co-NP, meaning every NP problem has an efficient verification for 'no' instances.
It proves that if P ≠ NP, there must exist NP-intermediate problems — neither in P nor NP-complete — and integer factorisation is a candidate.
quiz.explanation: Ladner's theorem (1975) proves that if P ≠ NP, then there exist problems in NP that are neither in P nor NP-complete — the 'NP-intermediate' zone. No problem has been proven NP-intermediate, but integer factorisation (the basis of RSA) and graph isomorphism are strong candidates: both are in NP, neither has a polynomial algorithm, and neither has been proven NP-complete. This three-tier structure (P / NP-intermediate / NP-complete) would exist only under P ≠ NP — another reason the question matters deeply.
